extracted.intended_audience: general readers of satire/humor and critics of Christian Science or religious movements
extracted.subtask_description: A satirical, essayistic critique (Mark Twain) examining Christian Science and similar 'mind-cure' movements, offering both moral/political commentary and practical observations about how such movements operate and succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanity standard: acceptance of basic truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who accept simple, self-evident facts (e.g., 'water seeks its level', 'the sun gives light and heat', basic arithmetic) are to be considered 'substantially sane' and entitled to go at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain presents a satirical 'infallible standard of sanity': whoever disputes any of these agreed-upon, elementary truths is judged 'wholly insane' and fit for the asylum. Use this as a tongue-in-cheek measure distinguishing 'working essentials' of sanity from mere opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insanity-as-difference-of-opinion rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In matters of opinion (especially political and religious) people who disagree with us are, by that fact, 'insane' from our point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a satirical observation about human tribalism: opinion disputes are 'brass-farthing' in value, and each side perceives the other as insane. The practical implication is a call for charity toward differing beliefs while recognizing mutual irrationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion-success criterion: must be a religion, not mere philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed broadly, a movement must be a religion rather than only a philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain argues that movements that become religions (with ritual, worship, etc.) have a better chance to attract wide followings and longevity than abstract philosophies alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion-success criterion: should not claim entire originality
rubrics_metrics.description: A new movement should not at first claim entire originality but present itself as an improvement on an existing religion, revealing its distinctiveness later when strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strategy makes newcomers more comfortable adopting the movement; Twain compares this to historic growth patterns (e.g., Mohammedanism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion-success criterion: must have money
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful movement needs money—'plenty of it'—to grow and exert influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain emphasizes financial resources as a decisive practical factor enabling activities like publishing, central organization, and political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion-success criterion: concentrate power and authority in a small clique
rubrics_metrics.description: Power and authority (and the handling of funds) must be concentrated in the grip of a small and irresponsible clique, with no outsiders privileged to ask questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized, unaccountable control enables rapid, cohesive decision-making and enforcement of orthodoxy; Twain treats this as a feature (though morally suspect) of movements that grow into powerful institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion-success criterion: bait the followers with attractive advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: A new movement must offer attractive, concrete advantages (e.g., present health, cheerfulness) to bait adherents away from competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain suggests that offering desirable worldly benefits—especially immediate ones—broadens appeal beyond the small audience that abstract doctrines attract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion-success criterion: introduce a new personage to worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing a new personage to worship (a living or charismatic figure) is a decisive advantage for a nascent religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain argues this feature has never before been combined so early and effectively with other requisites; a personage enables cult of personality, devotion, and monetization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization and monopolization of religious literature/goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mother-Church/Trust monopolizes production and sale of the movement's literature and requires purchases (e.g., 'Annex', Bible-Annex) and annual 'capitation tax' to retain membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain supplies concrete examples and prices (e.g., 'levan,t ... prepaid, $6') to show systematic commercialization: cash in advance, required purchases, and restrictions on who may legitimately publish or practice without Trust-approved materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety principle: forbidding medicines is dangerous; claiming too much is risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Sects that bar medicines yet claim ability to cure every ailment are dangerous and 'claim too much'; faith- and prayer-based cures that allow medicines probably 'do no harm' when they do no good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain distinguishes between harmless faith-cures that coexist with conventional care and those that forbid medical treatment, warning public confidence would increase 'if less were claimed.' He recommends that movements not overclaim curative power and not prohibit concurrent medical treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating testimonial evidence: prefer definite testimonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefinite or vague testimonies (e.g., 'saw spiritually') are unreliable and ought to be 'waste-basketed'; definite, specific cures are stronger evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain criticizes the magazine's poor editing for allowing ambiguous accounts; when assessing healing claims, demand concrete, verifiable details rather than emotional or vague statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of many 'mind cures': diversion of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Many cures attributed to mind/faith methods operate by diverting the patient's imagination into healthy channels—repetitive affirmative thought ('I am well!')—which can abolish imagined ailments for some people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain acknowledges psychological efficacy for certain sufferers, especially the religious, but notes this will not help all and may produce a false sense of omnipotence; it explains many recoveries without invoking supernatural powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy/ethical concern: protecting children from faith-only treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is problematic that the law allows parents to entrust their helpless children to faith-healers whose methods may exclude medical care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain relays correspondent protests that while adults may choose such risks, allowing children to be subjected without safeguard is a 'burning shame'—a point to consider in evaluating the ethics and legality of such movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/economic critique: lack of charitable spending
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trust appears to collect large sums but shows no evidence of spending on charities, orphans, hospitals, missions, libraries, etc.; this is a negative ethical indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain searched 'by correspondence and otherwise' and found no trace of benevolence expenditures, using this as a metric to criticize the movement's priorities and the Trust's devotion to 'the Dollar.'
